title: Storm Rachel Weakens but Keeps Soaking the Southwest
summary:
Rachel, a storm that brought flooding and damage to Southern California over the weekend, has weakened. On Sunday, the National Weather Service said Rachel had been downgraded to a post-tropical storm. That means it no longer has the structure of a tropical storm, but it can still bring heavy rain and wind.

As the storm moved inland across the desert Southwest, the weather service said the region was still at risk of flash floods. Strong waves called high surf were also expected to keep hitting coastal towns.

In California beach cities such as Long Beach and Newport Beach, big waves broke through sand walls, called berms, that had been built to keep the ocean back. Some oceanfront homes were partly underwater. Flood warnings covered much of the California coast, from San Diego up to the San Francisco Bay area.

Farther inland, rockslides blocked some roads for a while. Las Vegas broke a daily rainfall record on Sunday, and the weather service issued a flood watch for much of Utah, including Salt Lake City.

Forecasters warned that Rachel may be a preview of the months ahead. They expect this winter to bring the strongest El Niño on record. El Niño is a weather pattern in which parts of the Pacific Ocean become warmer than usual, which can change rain and storms around the world. Forecasters say it could bring record rainfall, huge waves and mudslides to California into next year.

California is getting ready. Last month, Governor Gavin Newsom issued an emergency proclamation to release money and resources. The state is putting more than 4 million sandbags in place, along with portable flood barriers and rock to repair levees, which are walls that hold back water. Workers are also inspecting dams and strengthening beach piers.
why_it_matters: Rachel shows how one storm can affect several states, and it may be an early sign of a stormy El Niño winter. Preparing early with sandbags, levee repairs and dam checks can help protect communities.

background_read: Tropical storms form over warm ocean water and get their energy from it, so they usually weaken after they move over land or cooler water.
Forecasters at the National Weather Service track storms and issue warnings and watches so people know when flooding is possible.
El Niño is a natural pattern in which parts of the Pacific Ocean warm up, shifting where heavy rain and storms are likely to fall.
Communities prepare for floods with sandbags, barriers and strong levees that help keep rising water away from homes.
